The list's stated value is that "an exemption is a reviewer's checklist item with a stated reason". Twenty-nine copies of an identical sentence are not a checklist — the premise the design rests on is contradicted by the data.

## What to change

Split the register:

1. `clause21Unowned` — a **membership golden** of the 29 names, one line each, with the reason stated once for the class. Exact-set matched against the obligation names whose section is 21.x, so it cannot drift and so adding a clause-21 name to the grammar reddens the build. That answers the doc's objection to widening ("a widened rule is invisible"): this widening is counted and diffed.
2. `carrierExemptions` — keeps the 6 genuine entries, each with its own reason and bead. That is the "handful" the doc asked for.

A membership golden rather than a count, per the corpus convention: a count would let one clause-21 name replace another silently.

**No ratchet on the clause-21 list.** `isoGaps` ratchets because an unimplemented ISO production is debt that must not grow. A clause-21 name is not debt — it means the grammar named another identifier production — so capping it would be a number that gets raised rather than a guard.

## Verification

Mutation sweep as with gqlc-cer/eh4/w2o: prove the exact-set match fires when a clause-21 name is added, removed, or moved between the two registers.
close_reason: Landed as PR #487 (squash 2026-07-28). carrierExemptions cut 35 -> 6; the 29 clause-21 names moved to clause21Unowned, a membership golden exact-set matched against the grammar by TestClause21Unowned. Mutation sweep: 10 mutations, 9 caught; the survivor (token attribution) is filed as gqlc-1uf.

title: schema/gql: perturb type arguments as well as remove them, to close the no-verdict hole
description:
TestNoUndeclaredLossiness (gqlc-eh4, PR #482) decides whether a resolving corpus file discards a parenthesised type argument by removing the argument and re-resolving: an identical model proves the argument reached nothing. Removal is sound but incomplete, because the bare spelling is not always grammatical, and an ungrammatical variant yields no verdict rather than a verdict of "lossless".

The demonstrated instance is DECIMAL. decimalExactNumericType (GQL.g4:1832) puts notNull? inside the parenthesised group, so `DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL` cannot become `DECIMAL NOT NULL` — that is a syntax error, the comparison never happens, and a file of that shape could hide a discard indefinitely. The same is true of DURATION: bare `DURATION` does not parse ("no viable alternative").

## What to change

Try a *perturbed* argument before falling back to removal. Probed and confirmed working:

- `DECIMAL(10,2)` vs `DECIMAL(11,3)` — parses, and the models collide, so the discard IS detectable this way
- `STRING(5)` vs `STRING(6)` — parses, collides
- `DURATION(DAY TO SECOND)` vs `DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH)` — parses, collides

A numeric perturbation is mechanically derivable: if the argument is made only of digits, commas, whitespace and 0x/0b/0o literals, substitute a different literal of the same shape. That covers every gqlc-5md and gqlc-h9n.31 case and is grammatical wherever the original is, because the argument's syntactic slot is unchanged.

## Residual after that

A non-numeric qualifier still needs a substitute nobody can derive — DURATION's field list is the known example, and its two files are already registered as semantic cases, so nothing is hiding there today. Either leave it as a stated limit or register the qualifier alternatives by hand; the former is probably right until a second non-numeric qualifier exists.

## Why it is P2 and not urgent

The sweep found nothing hiding behind this hole right now: every corpus file that spells a parenthesised argument is either declared lossy or is an unsupported entry. This closes a future gap, and makes the check's "no verdict" branch rare enough to be worth trusting.
notes:
PR #484 (branch test/w2o-perturb-type-arguments, commit eb55910). Replaced removal with a rewrite in discardedArguments; dropped removal entirely rather than keeping both.

Two findings beyond the bead's plan:

1. The hole was live. scalar_decimal_precision_scale.gql is a real corpus file removal could not reach, and the corpus had ALREADY worked around it by hand — that entry's semanticCases sibling is DECIMAL(8), with a comment explaining bare DECIMAL will not substitute. This makes mechanical what an author had derived manually.

2. Removal turned out to be redundant, not merely weaker. Probed every type keyword in the corpus vocabulary: none rejects T(1) while accepting bare T. So removal could not reach a case a rewrite misses. A mutation deleting the removal variant left the suite green, which is what settled it.

Verified by 10 mutations, 9 caught. W10 (strip the bead+reason+semanticCases row from scalar_decimal_precision_scale.gql and repin wantSemanticCases) was SILENT before this change and now reddens TestNoUndeclaredLossiness — that is the regression this bead existed to make visible.

W8 (drop the !ok guard) survived: DURATION() is not GQL either, so the outcome matches by accident of the grammar. Guard kept with a comment saying so rather than a claim it is witnessed.

Residual unchanged and stated in the test doc: a non-numeric qualifier has no derivable rewrite. DURATION's field list is the only instance and both files are registered (gqlc-8pe).
close_reason: Landed PR #484 (merged bed5030). Replaced argument removal with argument rewriting in TestNoUndeclaredLossiness, and dropped removal entirely rather than keeping both — probing showed no type in GQL's vocabulary rejects a rewritten argument while accepting a bare one, so removal could not reach a case a rewrite misses, and the mutation deleting it left the suite green. Verified by 10 mutations, 9 caught; the headline (W10) is that undeclaring scalar_decimal_precision_scale.gql was silent before and now reddens the gate. Residual stated in the test doc: a non-numeric qualifier has no derivable rewrite (DURATION's field list, both files already registered under gqlc-8pe).

title: ci: decide whether required_status_checks.strict should be on for master
description:
Split out of gqlc-0qu, which deliberately did not bundle it.

'Require branches to be up to date before merging' (required_status_checks.strict) is FALSE on master. Confirmed again 2026-07-27 while adding codegen-fence to the required contexts; strict was left as-is on purpose.

## Why it matters

With strict false, a PR's green CI can be computed against a base that no longer exists by the time it merges. Observed on PR #421: its CI was computed against a base that #422 had already replaced, and both touched internal/schema/gql. The combined tree was checked by hand and was fine — but nothing forced that check.

## Why it was not just turned on

Turning strict on serialises every merge: each PR must be rebased onto the new master and re-run CI after any other PR lands. With an autonomous loop merging several PRs an hour, and two loops running concurrently as of 2026-07-27, that could become the dominant cost.

## What to decide

Either accept the risk and record why in an ADR, or turn strict on and measure the added wall-clock per merge. A middle option: leave strict off but add a merge-time guard that refuses when the PR's base SHA is not an ancestor of current master AND the two touch overlapping paths.

Whichever is chosen, the reasoning belongs in an ADR, because the current state is an unrecorded default rather than a decision.
close_reason: Closed

title: ci: setup-just has no retry or cache — one network blip fails the job
description:
`.github/actions/setup-just/action.yml` installs the pinned `just` binary with a
bare `curl | bash` on every job of every workflow:

```
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://just.systems/install.sh \
  | bash -s -- --tag 1.55.1 --to "$HOME/.local/bin"
```

No retry, no cache. Every job therefore has two network single points of failure
(the install script, then the release tarball it fetches), and a transient reset
fails the job outright before a single test runs.

Observed 2026-07-27 on PR #443, job 89860643310, 15s in:

```
curl: (35) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
##[error]Process completed with exit code 35.
```

A `gh run rerun --failed` cleared it, which is the manual workaround; the
pipeline fix is to make the install survive a blip.

## Candidate fixes

- `--retry 5 --retry-all-errors --retry-delay 2` on the curl — one line, covers
  the script fetch. The tarball fetch inside `install.sh` is not covered by it,
  so this alone is partial.
- `actions/cache` on `~/.local/bin/just` keyed by the pinned version, with the
  curl as the cache-miss path. Removes the network from the steady-state run
  entirely and shaves the install off every job, which also helps wall time.

Prefer the cache, with the retry as belt-and-braces on the miss path. Note the
first run after adding a cache `path:` is cold by construction — judge steady
state on the second run, not the first.

## Acceptance

A CI run where the just install step is a cache hit and makes no network call,
plus a green run with the registry made unreachable on the miss path (or, less
strictly, the retry flags present and a documented rerun-free week).
close_reason: Shipped in PR #448. Added actions/cache@v4 keyed on just-1.55.1-OS with conditional install + curl retry flags.

title: schema/gql: corpus manifest lets lossy 'resolves' entries hide by omission
description:
corpus_test.go:385 gates the semanticCase requirement behind `if entry.bead != ""`. An entry that resolves lossily (discards a qualifier) but names no bead is structurally invisible to the check — the only assertion it faces is that its sentinel is nil. The guard catches bead-without-semantic-case; it cannot catch lossy-without-bead. Silence is a valid answer where it should not be.

## The incident

PR #439 (gqlc-h9n.4) shipped 11 entries flipped to `resolves`. Five of them (BINARY(4), BYTES(1, 10), VARBINARY(8), DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH), DURATION(DAY TO SECOND)) discard a declared qualifier — the same shape as the five pre-existing bead:gqlc-5md entries (CHAR(4), VARCHAR(10), STRING(5), STRING(2,5), DECIMAL(10,2)). All five walked through the gap on the first read, were caught by team-lead's pre-review, and were fixed in a follow-up commit on the same branch. The gap is demonstrated, not hypothetical, and demonstrated on a single commit.

## What to change

Make losslessness a positive declaration on the `resolves` outcome, not an omission. Design shape (author's call):

- add a `lossless bool` (or `losslessness lossy|lossless`) field on corpusEntry
- for outcome == resolves, require exactly one of: (lossless=true AND bead=="") OR (lossless=false AND bead!=""&&reason!=""&&semanticCase-row-exists)
- an unset `lossless` on a `resolves` entry is a test failure with a message that names the choice being demanded

Either shape closes the gap: the "I forgot to say" state stops being valid.

## Out of scope for gqlc-h9n.4

gqlc-h9n.4 is a schema/gql feature bead. Fixing the harness is a separate concern; the follow-up commit on that branch only fixes the entries that fell through. This bead tracks fixing the mechanism.
notes:
## Design: mechanical finder, not the declared field

The bead's suggested shape was a `lossless bool` / `losslessness lossy|lossless`
field on corpusEntry, required on every `resolves` entry. I built a mechanical
check instead, and the reason is that the declared field is not load-bearing.

Today `lossy` is exactly `bead != ""`: all 13 semantic cases are discarded
qualifiers (gqlc-5md length/precision/scale, gqlc-8pe duration qualifier,
gqlc-h9n.31 bit width), and the manifest already enforces resolving+bead ⟺
semanticCase. So the field would carry no information the bead field does not,
and 42 of the 55 resolving entries would gain a boilerplate `losslessness:
lossless` line. Its whole value would be the forcing function — and an author who
did not notice the qualifier will type `lossless` as readily as they typed
nothing. The gate would be theatre in exactly the shape gqlc-cer was chartered to
find.

TestNoUndeclaredLossiness takes the verdict off the author. For each resolving
entry with no bead it removes each parenthesised argument from the file and
re-resolves: a variant that produces the identical model proves the argument
reached nothing. The author declares nothing, and cannot lie.

## It found four live instances

The check was written against a green corpus and immediately failed on four
entries that were `resolves`, `mandatory`, no bead, no reason — the exact
"hide by omission" state, still present after PR #439's follow-up commit:

- 18.9-value-type/scalar_dec_alias.gql — DEC(8) collides with bare DEC
- 18.9-value-type/scalar_string_length_binary.gql — STRING(0b101) with STRING
- 18.9-value-type/scalar_string_length_hex.gql — STRING(0xFF) with STRING
- 18.9-value-type/scalar_string_length_octal.gql — STRING(0o17) with STRING

All four are gqlc-5md's discard (PropertyType has no length/precision field)
reached through spellings nobody had connected to it: DEC is DECIMAL's alias, and
the three base files exist to exercise the lexer's binary/hex/octal literals, so
their lossiness was incidental to why they were written. That is precisely the
row the bead predicted — "the one whose author did not think identity was at
stake". wantSemanticCases 13 → 17; the entry and resolving counts are unchanged.

## Limits, stated because the test cannot state them by passing

It is a search, not a proof. A variant that does not parse yields no verdict —
`DECIMAL NOT NULL` is not GQL, notNull? sitting inside the parenthesised group —
so a qualifier whose bare form is ungrammatical can still hide. The two duration
cases are of that shape; both are already registered, so nothing is lost today,
but the hole is real and a future qualifier could sit in it. The check also only
looks at parenthesised arguments, which is the only demonstrated shape of
lossiness in this model, not the only conceivable one.

## Verified by mutation (gqlc-cer's method)

Five mutations, all caught:
- un-register one of the four (drop bead, reason and its semanticCase row) →
  TestNoUndeclaredLossiness + TestCorpusSize
- discardedArguments returns nil → the positive witness fires
- discardedArguments reports everything it sees → the no-verdict witness fires
- the regex stops matching type arguments → the positive witness fires
- the no-verdict skip becomes a report → the no-verdict witness fires

The two witnesses exist because once the corpus is clean every file this test
examines has nothing to report, and a search that reports nothing is
indistinguishable from a search that looks for nothing.
close_reason: Landed PR #482. Built a mechanical finder rather than the proposed losslessness field: TestNoUndeclaredLossiness removes each parenthesised type argument from every resolving entry with no bead and re-resolves, treating an identical model as proof the argument was discarded. Declined the declared field because lossy is already exactly bead != "" (all 13 semantic cases are discarded qualifiers), so the field would carry no new information and would be only as good as the author's attention. The finder found four live instances hiding by omission — DEC(8), STRING(0b101), STRING(0xFF), STRING(0o17), all gqlc-5md's discard reached through spellings nobody had connected to it. wantSemanticCases 13 to 17. Verified by five mutations, all caught. Residual no-verdict hole filed as gqlc-w2o.

title: schema/gql: register ErrEdgeKindArcMismatch as a provisional deviation, resolve against ISO semantics
description:
`gqlc-h9n.3` (PR #432) adds sentinel `ErrEdgeKindArcMismatch`: an edge type
declaration whose `<edge kind>` contradicts its arc/connector direction is
rejected as unsupported. Two corpus entries move under it —
`18.3-edge-type/kind_undirected_arc_directed.gql` (UNDIRECTED + `->`) and
`18.3-edge-type/phrase_form_undirected_connector.gql` (DIRECTED + `~`, previously
`ErrUndirectedEdge`).

This is a **new deliberate deviation** and belongs in the gqlc-0ri register
alongside `ErrLabelImplication` / `ErrUndirectedEdge` / `ErrUnsupportedSource`.
It is not yet recorded in any ADR.

## Why this one is harder than the other three

The other three reject constructs we can argue have no faithful mapping onto the
openCypher/neo4j execution model, or reference catalog state a static generator
cannot see. This one is different: **the grammar accepts the contradictory
spelling.**

`UNDIRECTED EDGE TYPE ... CONNECTING (a TO b)` parses. Confirmed by probe
(2026-07-25, `/tmp/h9n2probe/leadconn`): `endpointPair` lists
`endpointPairDirected` first, and ANTLR's prediction for `endpointPair` sees only
the parenthesised token run — `edgeKind` is never consulted, because
`endpointPairPhrase` is a sibling of `edgeTypePhraseFiller` under
`edgeTypePhrase`. The spelling yields a DIRECTED endpoint pair with
`AMBIG alts={1,2} exact=true`.

So whether such a declaration is *valid ISO GQL* is not answerable from the
grammar. It is a Syntax-Rules / General-Rules question, and those live only in
the paid PDF. Three outcomes are possible and we cannot currently tell them
apart:

1. ISO forbids the contradiction — our rejection is conformant, no deviation at
   all, and the register entry should say so.
2. ISO specifies a winner (kind wins, or arc wins) — our rejection **rejects a
   valid ISO program**, which directly violates the owner principle "we should be
   able to accept any valid ISO GQL; we should not have our own GQLC flavour."
3. ISO leaves it implementation-defined — rejection is fine but must be listed in
   the implementation-defined register.

## What this bead must NOT do

Do not write an ADR that says "we decided to reject, reasoning below, standard
not consulted." Where the standard is the only possible arbiter, that phrasing
launders a coin-flip into documentation. A deviation record is honest when we
made a choice; it is not honest when we skipped the only source that could tell
us whether there was a choice to make.

Rejecting is a defensible *interim* posture — it fails loudly rather than
silently picking a reading, which is strictly better than the pre-h9n.3 behaviour
of resolving UNDIRECTED+`->` as though it were directed. Record it as interim and
provisional, blocked on the semantic text.

## Acceptance

- Register the sentinel in the gqlc-0ri deviation table, marked provisional.
- The sentinel's doc comment in `internal/schema/gql/errors.go` must not imply
  ISO backing for a decision we made ourselves. Reviewer on #432 has been asked
  to check this specifically.
- Resolve to outcome 1/2/3 once `gqlc-lir` (buy ISO/IEC 39075, CHF 227) is
  decided. Cross-check `-implementation-defined.xml` at
  standards.iso.org/iso-iec/39075/ed-1/en/ first — it is free, and if the
  contradiction is listed there, outcome 3 is confirmed without the purchase.
close_reason: ErrEdgeKindArcMismatch moved to standalone var with provisional doc comment; corpus bead fields updated to gqlc-xtq; PR #551 merged. ISO implementation-defined.xml checked (127 items, none for edge kind/arc mismatch) — confirmed outcome 3 ruled out.

title: ci: pin the iso.org free artefacts we cite, and detect drift
description:
Once we cite `ISO_IEC_39075(en).bnf.txt` and `ISO_IEC_39075(en)-features.xml`
as normative sources, the citations are only as good as the copies we checked
them against. Those files are served from a live URL with no version in the
path:

    https://standards.iso.org/iso-iec/39075/ed-1/en/

They can change under us silently. There is a concrete reason to expect they
will: **ISO/IEC 39075:2024/CD Cor 1 is at Committee Draft stage** as of
2026-01-06 (https://www.iso.org/standard/93701.html). When a corrigendum
publishes, the BNF and features files are the most likely artefacts to be
regenerated. A feature description changing, or a production gaining an
alternative, would silently invalidate citations we had already landed.

## What to do

Record a checksum of each artefact we cite, alongside the fetch date, and add
a check that the live file still matches. On mismatch the check should fail
loudly and name the file — a corrigendum landing is a thing we want to know
about, not a thing to auto-accept.

## Open question that must be answered first — do not skip it

**Whether the ISO Customer Licence permits vendoring these files into a public
git repository is not established.** The licence text grants use "in their
original format without any modifications for the purposes specified in their
respective ISO standard(s)". That is plausibly a use grant rather than a
redistribution grant, and the two readings lead to different designs:

- **If vendoring is permitted:** commit the files, diff against the live copy
  in CI. Simple, hermetic, no network in the common path.
- **If it is not:** commit only the checksums and fetch at check time. That
  puts a network dependency in CI, so it must not be on the PR-blocking path
  — an ISO outage would then block all merges. Run it on a schedule instead
  and open an issue on drift.

Resolve the licence question before writing any code. Getting this wrong in
the permissive direction means committing a third party's copyrighted artefact
to a public repo, which is not a defect we can fix by reverting.

## Scope note

This is infrastructure for `gqlc-cfj` (Annex D feature ids) and the ISO-BNF
coverage gate. It is not a blocker for either — both can land citing the URL
and the fetch date. File this as the durable version of that citation.
close_reason: Closed

title: ci: gate that a PR body carries Closes #N when its bead has an external_ref
description:
Two PRs in one session (#421 h9n.16, #422 h9n.18) opened with no `Closes #N`
line at all. Both were caught by hand at merge time. Different authors, same
omission, so this is a missing gate rather than two mistakes.

## Why it matters

Beads IDs in a PR body do not auto-close the mirrored GitHub issue — GitHub
only recognises `Closes` / `Fixes` / `Resolves` plus the **GH issue number**.
When the line is absent the PR merges, the bead gets closed by the lead, and
the GH issue silently stays open. The repo accumulates open issues whose work
shipped weeks ago, and the bd↔GH mirror stops being trustworthy in the
direction people actually read it.

The existing memory `pr-body-closes-gh-issue` covers getting the *number*
right. That is a different failure. Here the line was simply never written, so
no amount of number-checking would have caught it.

## What the gate cannot be

Not a blanket "every PR body must contain Closes #N". Three legitimate
exceptions:

- `chore(bd)` export-sync PRs map to no issue at all.
- Child PRs under an epic must **not** close the umbrella issue. `gqlc-h9n` is
  `#359` and closing it early would wipe the epic's tracking.
- Infra/tooling PRs filed without a bead.

A gate that fires on those trains people to ignore it, which is worse than no
gate.

## Shape that works

Derive the obligation from the bead, not from the PR:

1. Extract the bead id from the PR body (`Bead: gqlc-xxx` is the house
   convention) or the branch name. If there is none, PASS — nothing to check.
2. `bd show <id>` → read the `External:` link. If the bead has no external_ref,
   PASS.
3. If it has one, require `Closes #<that exact number>` in the body. FAIL
   naming both the bead and the number if absent, and FAIL differently if a
   `Closes #M` is present with M ≠ N — that is the wrong-close case
   `workflow-verify-bd-gh-mapping-before-closes` describes, and it is worse
   than absence because it closes someone else's issue.
4. Exempt beads whose type is `epic`, so umbrella issues can never be targeted.

Step 4 is the load-bearing one. Without it the gate would demand `Closes #359`
on every child PR of the epic and actively cause the harm it exists to prevent.

## Notes for whoever takes this

- Needs `bd` available in CI, or the external_ref has to come from the
  committed `.beads/issues.jsonl` export instead. The export is the cheaper
  read and is already in the tree — but note it is a *passive* export and can
  be stale, so a bead filed in the same session as the PR may not be in it yet.
  If that turns out to be common, PASS on unknown-bead rather than FAIL, and
  say so in the message; a gate that blocks on its own staleness gets disabled.
- Mutation-test it against #421 and #422 as they were at open time (bodies with
  no `Closes` line) and confirm it FAILS naming `#403` and `#401`. Then against
  #423 (`chore(bd)`, no bead) and confirm PASS.
- Fold into an existing job. This is one `bd show` and one grep.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #450. New .github/scripts/check-pr-closes.py + step folded into tidy job.

title: BLOCKED (no ISO arbiter, gqlc-lir): retire or confirm ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties against ISO 18.3
description:
> **BLOCKED — permanently, as of 2026-07-27. Do not resolve this by inference.**
>
> This question is answerable only from ISO/IEC 39075's General Rules, which are
> in the paid PDF. `gqlc-lir` decided against the CHF 227 purchase, so there is
> no arbiter and there will not be one. The free BNF positively proves the
> ambiguity is not resolvable syntactically.
>
> A web-search paraphrase, a vendor conformance table, or an analogy to SQL is
> **not** a citation. If gqlc must pick a behaviour to ship, record it as a gqlc
> decision under gqlc's own name — never as "ISO says" — and leave this bead
> open, because the standards question stays unanswered either way.

Opened 2026-07-26 alongside PR #422, which introduces
`ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties`. That sentinel is correct today but may be
provisional, and this bead holds the evidence needed to decide.

## What #422 settled and what it did not

Before #422, an inline endpoint filler carrying properties —
`(:Person)-[:AUTHORED]->(:Post { extra :: STRING })` — parsed, resolved with
`err=nil`, and produced a model byte-identical to the label-only spelling. The
property declarations had no consumer and were discarded. That is the epic's
signature defect: accepted input, nil error, wrong model.

#422 rejects the spelling instead. What it did NOT settle is what the spelling
*means*, and the implementer was explicit that the grammar does not adjudicate:

- **Declaration reading.** `propertyType` is `propertyName typed?
  propertyValueType` — that is declaration syntax, not constraint syntax. On
  this reading the filler declares properties on the endpoint node type, and
  supporting it needs merge-and-conflict semantics against the standalone
  declaration of that node type.
- **Reference reading.** Alt 2 of `sourceNodeTypeReference` /
  `destinationNodeTypeReference` (GQL.g4:1620/1625) strips both the
  `nodeSynonym TYPE? nodeTypeName` prefix and the `localNodeTypeAlias?` from
  the full `nodeTypePattern`. CONTEXT.md:50 already codifies the endpoint as
  "resolved to the referenced node type's label set". On this reading the
  properties are a constraint over something declared elsewhere.

The load-bearing observation, and the reason #422 could land without waiting:
**accept-and-discard is not correct under either reading**, so the sentinel is
right now regardless of how this resolves.

## What this bead must produce

The ISO/IEC 39075:2024 subclause 18.3 semantic sentence for alt 2 of
`<source node type reference>` / `<destination node type reference>`. A
citation, not an inference — `gqlc-cfj` is open because this repo has a habit of
asserting what the standard says without sourcing it, and the two readings above
are exactly the kind of gap that gets filled by plausible-sounding reasoning.

Then one of:

1. **Declaration.** Implement merge semantics against the standalone
   declaration, and decide what a *conflicting* redeclaration does (same
   property name, different value type). Lift the sentinel. Note this drags in
   whatever gqlc decides about one-graph-type-per-file scoping.
2. **Constraint.** Implement satisfaction-checking: the referenced node type
   must already declare a compatible property signature, else a *different*
   error — a constraint violation, not an unsupported-construct rejection.
   Overlaps gqlc-h9n.22 (plural label satisfaction, property intersection),
   which is the same shape of question one level up. Sequence after it.
3. **Standard does not specify.** Keep the sentinel permanently, record it in
   the gqlc-0ri deviation register, and rewrite the error's doc comment from
   "not yet supported" to a stated deviation. Silence in the standard is itself
   the finding and must be written down, not left as an open bead forever.

## Guardrails for whoever takes this

- The retirement must be a **local** change. #422 was reviewed on the claim that
  lifting the sentinel later is not a redesign. If implementing (1) or (2) turns
  out to require restructuring how endpoints resolve, that invalidates a premise
  of #422's review and should come back to team-lead rather than being absorbed
  quietly.
- `(:Post {})` with empty braces is deliberately ACCEPTED and pinned by
  `TestEndpointFillerEmptyBraceAllowed`. Any widening must keep that pin green —
  it exists because an ANTLR accessor is non-nil for the empty-braces form, so a
  nil-check guard would over-reject. Do not regress it into an existence test.
- Symmetry is a stated invariant: source and destination behave identically,
  including under left-pointing-arc canonicalisation. Whatever replaces the
  sentinel keeps that property or explains why not.
notes:
HELD UNLABELLED PERMANENTLY by Սեդրակ 2026-08-21 — and this one must not be 'tidied up' later.
This bead is a genuine unknown that cannot be answered from anything we own. Its blocker
gqlc-lir is CLOSED as 'no buy' (Անդրանիկ declined the CHF 227 for ISO/IEC 39075), and that
close reason says in terms: 'h9n.28, h9n.29 and the semantic half of 0ri stay open as
permanently-blocked honest unknowns; they must not be resolved by inference.'
THE HAZARD THE KINGDOM INTRODUCED. Because gqlc-lir is CLOSED, bd does not consider this bead
blocked — it sits in bd ready. Under the dispatcher, a labelled bead in bd ready gets a warrior
woken on it, and a warrior woken on an unanswerable question will answer it by inference,
because that is the only way to make progress. That is precisely the failure Անդրանիկ's
decision forbids. The prose 'BLOCKED' in the title stops a human; it stops no dispatcher.
So: NEVER label this class:*. The absent label is the only thing standing between this bead
and an inferred answer entering the record as fact.
I have deliberately NOT set it to deferred, which would drop it out of bd ready and be the
tidier mechanism: Անդրանիկ's decision says these STAY OPEN, and that decision predates the
kingdom. Changing the state to work around my own dispatcher is not mine to do unilaterally.
I will put the question to him: does 'stay open' mean 'open in the ledger', or did he mean
'unresolved', in which case deferred is the honest state and the ready queue stops lying.

comments.author: areqag
comments.text:
2026-07-26, team-lead. Same verdict as gqlc-h9n.28: BLOCKED ON ISO PURCHASE, not on research.

ISO's free normative BNF (https://standards.iso.org/iso-iec/39075/ed-1/en/, verified by fetch) confirms the two-alternative structure this bead is about, verbatim at line 1250:

    <source node type reference> ::=
        <left paren> <source node type alias> <right paren>
      | <left paren> [ <node type filler> ] <right paren>

    <destination node type reference> ::=
        <left paren> <destination node type alias> <right paren>
      | <left paren> [ <node type filler> ] <right paren>

So the second alternative really does admit a full <node type filler> — the bead's premise is sourced, not assumed. But whether that filler DECLARES a node type or REFERENCES one is a semantic question the BNF cannot answer, and both readings stay viable. Subclause 18.3's General Rules are the arbiter and they are in the paid PDF only.

Difference from h9n.28, and why this one is lower stakes: PR #422 already fixed the immediate defect (endpoint fillers carrying properties were being accepted and discarded — accepted input, nil error, wrong model). What remains is only whether ErrEndpointFillerHasProperties should be RETIRED, i.e. whether we are currently rejecting something the standard permits. Rejecting a valid construct is a visible, loud failure that a user can report; it is not the silent-wrong-model class. So this does not on its own justify the CHF 227.

Recommendation: hold at current state. If the standard is purchased for h9n.28, resolve this in the same sitting — the marginal cost is one subclause read.

title: test(schema): gate resolving-path incidental carriers, not just parse-time ones
description:
Found 2026-07-26 by the gqlc-h9n.17 non-vacuity check, which is the best kind of
finding: the new gate was run against the two historical orphans it was meant to
prevent, reproduced one, and did NOT reproduce the other.

## The two carriage classes

`gqlc-h9n.17` gates **parse-time** incidental carriage: a grammar name that the
whole corpus reaches but that no file in the *owning* area reaches. Verified by
replay at `0b000c60` (parent of the TIMESTAMP fix), where it correctly reports
`localdatetimeType#2 (alt) owned by D1, D2`.

Replayed at `22e02c02` (has the TIMESTAMP fix, lacks the NODE-synonym fix
`7217b180`) it **passes**, i.e. it does not catch the NODE orphan. That is not a
bug in h9n.17. The `NODE` token IS entered at that SHA — by
`18.2-node-type/phrase_form.gql` and `18.9-value-type/constructed_node_closed.gql`
— so parse coverage is genuinely satisfied. But **both of those files are
`unsupported`**: the listener rejects them after the parse succeeds, so nothing
downstream of the parse tree ever sees the name.

`7217b180`'s own commit message says it exactly: "no *resolving* path exercised
an explicit node synonym in nodeTypePattern".

So there are two distinct classes and we currently gate one:

- **parse-time carriage** — some file's parse tree enters the name. GATED by
  h9n.17.
- **resolving-path carriage** — some file that actually *resolves* enters the
  name. NOT GATED. A name can be carried exclusively by files that are expected
  to fail, and every existing gate stays green.

The second class is strictly the more dangerous one, because "the only files
exercising this construct are ones we reject" is a coverage illusion that reads
as coverage in every report we currently produce.

## Why it was not folded into h9n.17

h9n.17's method spec is written in terms of the coverage gate, which measures
the parse tree. Measuring resolving-path carriage needs a different instrument:
run `Parse` (not just the parser) over every corpus file, keep only the files
whose outcome is `resolves`, and recompute carriage over that subset. That is a
second traversal with different inputs, not a parameter on the existing one.

## Sketch

Plausibly cheap: `carried_resolving(area)` = carriage computed over
`{f in area : outcome(f) == resolves}`, compared against the same
section-derived ownership map h9n.17 already builds. The ownership machinery,
the exemption list, and the orphan-reporting format are all reusable as-is;
only the file filter changes.

Open question worth deciding before implementing: should the obligation set for
the resolving gate be the same grammar closure? A construct we deliberately
reject (see gqlc-h9n.6) can never have a resolving carrier, so the resolving
gate would report it as a permanent orphan. Either the obligation set is
narrowed to resolvable constructs, or every deliberate rejection needs an
exemption — and the second option turns the exemption list into a duplicate of
the sentinel registry. Prefer the first, but measure how many names it moves
before committing to it.

Relates to gqlc-h9n.13 (parse-shape recording promoted from report to gate) and
gqlc-h9n.24 (the manifest cannot express a changed-but-still-resolving model).
All three are the same underlying complaint: our instruments measure the parse
tree, and most of the defects this epic finds live downstream of it.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #465. TestCorpusResolvingCarriers gates resolving-path carriage in two tiers: corpus-wide (does any resolving file reach the name) and per-area (does the owning area). The bead's open question, answered by measurement first: neither listed option survives. Narrowing the obligation to resolvable constructs is VACUOUS on the motivating case — before 7217b180 no file spelling NODE resolved, so a corpus-derived narrowing would have dropped NODE and missed the defect. Per-name exemptions would be ~89 entries carrying 89 copies of 7 reasons. Shipped: full obligation kept, excuse derived from the sentinel (7 accounts), names still listed as the pin, and the account itself checked — every carrier of a listed name must reject with that exact sentinel. Tier 2 found a real gap on first run: 18.3-edge-type owns the alias endpoint alternatives but every area-C file reaching them was unsupported; pattern_endpoint_alias.gql closes it. Also corrected six carrier exemptions that wrongly claimed this gate would retire them (verified by mutation: they are structurally unowned by section prefix).

title: schema/gql: non-power-of-two binary precision (INT(7)) silently widens to machine int — decide and record
description:
Noticed 2026-07-26 while ratifying the gqlc-h9n.16 width fold. Not a blocker for
that bead — this behaviour is byte-identical before and after the fold — but the
fold makes the question unavoidable, so record the answer rather than inherit it.

## The question

`GQL.g4:1801` is `INT (LEFT_PAREN precision RIGHT_PAREN)? notNull?`, under
`binaryExactNumericType`. Precision there is a **bit width** (that is what
separates `binaryExactNumericType` from `decimalExactNumericType`, whose
precision pairs with a `scale` — GQL.g4:1788 vs 1831).

`INT(8)` has an exact counterpart in the model (`TypeInt8`) and gqlc-h9n.16
folds it. `INT(7)` does not. Today, and after h9n.16, it canonicalises to `INT`
and resolves to `graph.TypeInt` — a machine int. The schema author said seven
bits; the model says sixty-four, silently.

That is precisely what ADR 0002's rationale forbids:

  "Losing signedness and width would force codegen to emit int/uint everywhere
   and discard information the schema author explicitly stated."

So the status quo for non-power-of-two widths contradicts the same sentence that
justifies fixing the power-of-two ones. h9n.16 fixes the half with an exact
model counterpart and leaves the other half exactly as it was.

## Why it was not just fixed inside h9n.16

The obvious fix — reject `INT(7)` with `ErrUnsupportedType` — collides with a
standing project directive: *if it is valid ISO GQL, we should allow it; we do
not get our own gqlc flavour.* `INT(7)` is valid ISO GQL. Narrowing acceptance
to protect model fidelity trades one stated goal against another, and that
trade needs a decision, not an implementer's judgement call at edit time.

## Candidate resolutions

1. **Status quo, recorded.** `INT(7)` -> `TypeInt`. Accepts everything valid;
   loses the stated width. Requires an entry in the gqlc-0ri deviation register
   saying so out loud, and a comment at the fallback in
   `internal/schema/gql/propertytype.go` naming it lossy.
2. **Round up to the next supported width.** `INT(7)` -> `TypeInt8`,
   `INT(10)` -> `TypeInt16`, `INT(24)` -> `TypeInt32`. Representationally safe
   in the sense that the wider type holds every value of the narrower one, and
   loses far less than jumping to 64. BUT it depends on reading precision as a
   *minimum* capacity ("at least p bits") rather than an exact one. Nobody here
   has sourced that from ISO 39075, and gqlc-cfj is an open bead about exactly
   this habit of citing the standard without sourcing it. Do not adopt this
   without a citation.
3. **Reject.** `ErrUnsupportedType` for any precision without an exact model
   counterpart. Maximum fidelity, violates the accept-all-valid-GQL directive.

## What to do

Pick one and write it down. If the answer is (1) — which is the cheapest and
the current behaviour — that is a fine answer, but it has to be *stated*, because
right now a reader of ADR 0002 would reasonably predict (3) and a reader of the
project directive would reasonably predict (1), and nothing in the tree
adjudicates.

Applies equally to `UINT(p)`, `INTEGER(p)`, and `FLOAT(p)` for any p without an
exact counterpart. `DECIMAL(p,s)` is NOT in scope: its precision is decimal
digits, not bits, and it is gqlc-5md's problem.
close_reason:
Decided in docs/adr/0017-off-lattice-binary-widths-accepted-and-lost.md, PR #463
(squash 3ba0f7b… see origin/master), merged 2026-07-28.

## The answer: option 1, accept and record

INT(7) / INT(10) / UINT(p) / INTEGER(p) at any width PropertyType cannot express
resolve to the unqualified type. FLOAT(p) likewise at every p.

## Why, in one paragraph

ADR 0016's discriminator (an undirected edge answers IS DIRECTED *incorrectly*,
so rejecting removes a wrong answer) does not transfer, and the reason is about
what the alternative costs rather than what is lost. For INT(7), the alternative
to accepting is not compiling the schema at all: a property declaration is one
line inside a graph type, and rejecting it takes down every node type, edge type
and other property in the file to suppress one discarded qualifier. Rejecting
does not make gqlc right about the width — it makes gqlc unable to say anything.

The nearest analogue to IS DIRECTED was checked rather than assumed away:
valueTypePredicate (GQL.g4:2052, `<value expression> IS [NOT] TYPED <value
type>`) is real, takes a valueExpressionPrimary — a *value*, where what gqlc
discards is a *declaration* — and gqlc has no GQL query surface (ADR 0007). The
residual "could ISO's General Rules reach a declared type" is paywalled
(gqlc-lir) and is flagged in the ADR as a hedge, not offered as proof. The
decision does not rest on it.

Option 2 (round up) declined twice over: it reads precision as a minimum, which
nobody has sourced — this bead's own instruction, gqlc-h9n.28's standing rule,
gqlc-cfj's open habit-bead — and it buys no correctness anyway, since a signed
7-bit value in an int8 is the same permissive-imprecise wrong in a smaller
quantity.

Option 3 (reject) also answered against ADR 0006's conservatism argument, which
a reviewer will reach for: that asymmetry is about gqlc's own inferences.
Narrowing the accepted *language* is a different act — a rejection of valid ISO
GQL is not a default that can be relaxed later, it is a gqlc dialect for as long
as it stands.

## Delivered beyond what was asked

The bead asked for a comment at the propertytype.go fallback and a deviation
register entry. Both done, but the loss is now *asserted* rather than described,
using the siblings machinery from gqlc-h9n.21 (PR #461):

- scalar_signed_integer.gql — INT(10), siblings INT / INTEGER / INTEGER(10) / INT(7)
- scalar_unsigned_integer.gql — UINT(10), siblings UINT / UINT(7)
- scalar_float.gql — FLOAT(10), siblings FLOAT / FLOAT(10, 2)

INT(8) is deliberately absent from that class: it folds, and its absence is the
contrast that shows the loss is jagged rather than uniform. Verified by mutation
both ways — adding INT(8) reddens TestSemanticCaseCollisions on exactly that
subtest; deleting an entry's bead/reason while leaving its semanticCase reddens
TestCorpusManifest. wantSemanticCases 10 -> 13.

## Register correction

gqlc-0ri gains no table row, and has a note saying why: its table is one row per
*rejection sentinel*, and this decision adds no rejection. A row there would be
the half-wrong row ADR 0016 declined to write when it split ErrUnsupportedSource.

## Follow-up filed

gqlc-h9n.31 — declared bit width on PropertyType, third sibling to gqlc-5md and
gqlc-8pe, blocked on the same bar (name the consumer first). Sibling rather than
part of gqlc-5md because the model here *has* a width axis and quantises it, and
because integer widths are ordered and nested, making "unify to the wider" an
available answer with no counterpart for string lengths.

gqlc-h9n.28 is unaffected and stays open; answering it could move FLOAT(p)'s
ownership from gqlc-h9n.31 to gqlc-5md.

title: test(schema): the corpus manifest cannot express "resolves to a different right thing now"
description:
Surfaced 2026-07-26 while designing gqlc-h9n.16 (Problem A, the width fold).

## The gap

A corpus entry's `outcome` records whether a file parses, resolves, or is
rejected. It cannot express **"this file resolves to a DIFFERENT right thing
after this change than it did before"**.

Concretely: after the width fold, a file declaring `x :: INTEGER(8)` resolves
before AND after. Outcome is `resolves` in both cases. The manifest is satisfied
by both. But the model it resolves to changes from `TypeInt` to `TypeInt8` —
which is the entire point of the change, and the corpus is blind to it.

This is the same blindness as gqlc-uhb (phrase forms parsed and silently
discarded) seen from the other side. There, a wrong model hid behind a passing
`resolves`. Here, a *newly correct* model hides behind the same passing
`resolves`, so the corpus cannot certify that the fix took effect, and — worse —
could not have caught a regression that silently un-fixed it later.

## Why this is not a duplicate of gqlc-h9n.13

gqlc-h9n.13 promotes **parse-shape** recording from report to gate. Parse shape
is unchanged here: `INTEGER(8)` parses identically before and after the fold.
The divergence is entirely downstream of the parse tree, in normalisation. A
parse-shape gate would not fire.

## Why this is not a duplicate of gqlc-h9n.21

gqlc-h9n.21 asserts the model collision a `semanticCase` *describes*. That is a
mechanism for cases the harness already knows are about model identity. This
bead is about ordinary corpus rows, whose whole contract today is an outcome
string.

## Candidate shapes (not yet decided)

1. An optional `model:` assertion on a corpus row — a small structural
   fingerprint (property name -> resolved type constant) checked when present.
   Cheap; opt-in; only as good as the rows that opt in.
2. A golden model snapshot per corpus file, diffed in CI. Catches everything,
   including changes nobody thought to assert; costs a rebaseline ritual on
   every intentional change, which gqlc-exl already shows is expensive here.
3. Leave the corpus alone and require every normalisation change to carry its
   own pin table (which is what gqlc-h9n.16 Problem A does). Zero machinery;
   relies on author discipline; the failure mode is silent.

Option 3 is the status quo. The bead exists to decide whether that is
deliberate. Record the decision either way — if the answer is "the corpus is a
coverage instrument, not a model-identity instrument", that belongs in writing
next to the manifest, because two beads have now independently expected
otherwise.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #464. Decision recorded next to the manifest: the corpus is a coverage instrument, not a model-identity instrument. Option 1 (opt-in model: field) is only as good as the rows that opt in; option 2 (golden snapshots) is ruled out by gqlc-exl's evidentiary-circularity doctrine. Shipped option 3 mechanised: TestTypeSpellingsEveryRowPinned computes a grounding closure over hand-written pin/equivalence tables and fails while any typeSpellings row lacks an end-to-end assertion. Filled three real gaps (FLOAT32/64/128). DURATION needed no exemption — DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH) grounds it via the same truncateParenthetical fallback the production code takes. Verified by three mutations.

title: resolver: plural label satisfaction — property intersection, whole-entity rejection, and the ADR
description:
Step 2 of the gqlc-h9n.7 split. Step 1 makes subset matching work but refuses
any query whose label set is satisfied by two or more declared node types. This
bead makes the plural case resolve.

## The rule

A query label expression resolves to the **set** of declared node types whose
label set is a superset of it (with an exact match winning outright, per step 1).
Where that set is plural:

- a **property** reference resolves to the **intersection** — identical name,
  type and nullability across every member, else `ErrUnknownProperty`;
- a **whole-entity** reference (`RETURN p`) is **rejected**.

The property half is not a new commitment: `unionProperty`
(`internal/resolver/resolve.go:731`) already implements exactly this for
multi-candidate edges, including the type-mismatch case
(`resolve.go:744-746`). Substitute `[]schema.NodeType` for `[]schema.EdgeKey`.
Probed behaviour on the edge lane today:

    match (a:A)-[r:R|S]->(b:B) return r.w      -> OK, INT
    match (a:A)-[r:R|S]->(b:B) return r.only   -> unknown property: missing on union member A-[S]->B
    match (a:A)-[r:R|S]->(b:B) return r.skew   -> unknown property: type differs: property:INT vs property:STRING

## Why whole-entity is rejected rather than unioned

The obvious move is to copy the edge side's synthesised sealed interface
(`type TR interface{ isTR() }` with a `switch rel.Type` dispatch). **It does not
carry over, and this is the crux of the bead.** The edge dispatch is total
because a Neo4j relationship has exactly one type, so `rel.Type` is a single
string. The node analogue would dispatch on `dbtype.Node.Labels`, which is a
**set**, and under the very superset rule this bead introduces one runtime node
can satisfy two declared types at once: a node labelled
`{Person, Employee, Contractor}` conforms to both `Person&Employee` and
`Person&Contractor`. "First match wins" makes the emitted struct depend on map
ordering and there is no honest `default`.

The considered alternative was a per-query **intersection struct** carrying only
the common properties. It is implementable and total (decode the intersection
directly, no dispatch) — it is not blocked, only expensive: a new codegen entity
kind with its own naming rule, decode function and collision check against
schema entity names. It is rejected **for now** on the ADR 0006 argument:
widening a rejected query to an accepted one is non-breaking; replacing an
emitted struct that user code already names is not.

## Ripple — this is the bulk of the work

Pluralising the node lane is unavoidable and drags the edge endpoint lane with
it. `endpointLabels` (`resolve.go:503`) returns one `graph.LabelSetKey` read
from `resolved[v] -> nt.Labels`; `closeEdge`, `edgeCandidates`,
`candidateTypes` and `describeTriedEdges` all consume that single key. So
`scope.nodeTypes` goes from `map[string]schema.NodeType` to a candidate lane
mirroring `edgeCands`.

Counted: 20 `nodeTypes[...]` access sites in non-test code (`scope.go`,
`resolve.go`). 13 are presence-only (`_, ok :=`) and survive untouched. **7 read
the value and must each decide what plural means**: `scope.go:144` (BindNode's
`ErrPartBindingTypeConflict` identity compare), `:654` (`refProjectionType`),
`:807` (`Export`), `:918` (`PropertyUseWitness`), and `resolve.go:972` / `:1057`
/ `:1130` (SET / REMOVE / DELETE property validators) — plus `endpointLabels`.

Once the node lane exposes a set, the endpoint predicate composes cleanly:
"does declared `(:Person&Employee)-[:KNOWS]->(...)` match `(a:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(...)`"
is just "is `Person&Employee` in the satisfying set of `{Person}`" — the same
predicate reused. `edgeCandidates` becomes a cross-product over
src-set x labels x tgt-set x orientations. Cost is combinatorial, not
conceptual; schemas are small and `labelDeclared` (`resolve.go:1166`) already
documents naive iteration as a deliberate choice.

## ADR

**This bead carries an ADR; step 1 does not.** The plural decision picks a
permanent shape for the type model and, per ADR 0010, that shape leaks into
generated code users name. ADR 0006's argument — the conservative default is
safe because relaxing later is non-breaking and the reverse is not — decides
this one too, which is why it belongs in the same series. ADR 0006 is 64 lines;
this need not be longer.

Also fold in here: a runtime node labelled `{Person, Employee}` matches the
pattern `(:Person)` and is decoded as the `Person` struct, silently dropping
`employeeId`/`title`. That unsoundness predates this epic and step 1 neither
adds nor removes it, but the ADR is where it gets stated rather than left
implicit.
notes:
## Step-2 caveat from the designer's post-implementation pass (2026-07-26)

Two additions after reviewing the step-1 implementation (`160a4bf`).

**1. Exact precedence is a provisional tie-break, not the satisfaction rule.**
Step 1 resolves an exact `s.Nodes[key]` hit outright and only consults the
superset-satisfying set on a miss. That is correct for step 1 — it preserves
observable behaviour exactly, so the change is strictly widening. But under
ISO 39075 §16.8 **both** an exact type and a superset type satisfy the queried
label set, so precedence *hides* the plural case rather than resolving it.

Step 2 must explicitly reopen it. The hazard is that it is invisible: **no
fixture under `test/data/resolver/{valid,invalid}/schemas/` declares `&` at
all**, so nothing exercises the disagreement. A step-2 implementer who does not
know precedence was provisional will inherit it as settled semantics without
ever seeing a test that questions it. The ADR should record it as a step-1
tie-break and say plainly that step 2 revisits it.

**2. A sharper statement of the soundness hazard than this bead's description
carries.** The description above says a `{Person, Employee}` node decoded as the
`Person` struct silently drops `employeeId`/`title`. That understates it. The
worse direction is a **missing property flowing into a typed field**:

    (:Person        { id, name, email })
    (:Person&Employee { employeeId, title })     -- no email

`MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.email` types `email` as `STRING` from the bare
`Person` type. At runtime that pattern also matches `:Person:Employee` nodes,
which carry no `email` at all. So the generated code has a typed field fed by a
property the matched node may not possess — not an extra field discarded, but a
declared field with nothing behind it.

This **pre-dates the epic** and step 1 neither adds nor removes it. It is
recorded here because it is the strongest argument that plural whole-entity
projection must be *rejected* rather than papered over, and because it is the
kind of thing that reads as a step-2 implementation detail until someone ships
a nil deref.

## Agent triage 2026-07-28: blocked on an owner decision, not on effort

Claimed, scoped, then stood down — this bead's ADR is not in the delegated set,
and the undecided half of it gates the implementation rather than merely
documenting it. Recording the fork so it can be settled quickly.

**The fork: does exact-match precedence survive step 2?**

`resolveNodeLabels` (resolve.go:1195) returns `s.Nodes[labels.Key()]` outright on
an identity hit and only computes the satisfying set on a miss. NOTES point 1
above calls that a provisional step-1 tie-break and says step 2 must reopen it.
It is not reopened here, and the two answers are not close:

- **(A) Keep precedence.** An exact identity hit resolves singular; the plural
  lane only runs when no declared type's identity equals the queried set. The
  bead's rule (property intersection, whole-entity rejection) applies only in
  that residue.
- **(B) Satisfaction is satisfaction.** Drop the fast path; the satisfying set is
  the answer whether or not one member matches exactly. This is what ISO 39075
  §16.8 says — `:Person` is satisfied by any element whose label set contains
  Person, and a `Person&Employee` element is such an element.

**One existing fixture decides between them, and it is a live instance of NOTES
point 2's soundness hazard.** `test/data/resolver/valid/label_satisfy_exact_wins.cypher`
is `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p.name` against `valid/schemas/satisfy_singular.gql`,
which declares `(:Person { id, name })` and `(:Person&Employee { employeeId, title })`
— no `name` on the second.

- Under (A) it stays valid: `p.name` types as `STRING NOT NULL` off bare Person.
  At runtime the pattern also matches `:Person:Employee` nodes, which carry no
  `name`. That is precisely "a declared field with nothing behind it".
- Under (B) it becomes invalid: `name` is missing on a satisfying member, so the
  intersection rejects with ErrUnknownProperty — and the hazard is closed by
  construction.

So (B) is the conformant and sound answer, and it **narrows an accepted query to
a rejected one** — the direction ADR 0006's argument says to be careful about.
That is an owner call, not an agent call. The fixture's name already encodes (A),
which is why an implementer who does not read NOTES will inherit it as settled.

**Correction to NOTES point 1.** It says "no fixture under
test/data/resolver/{valid,invalid}/schemas/ declares `&` at all". Stale — step 1
(160a4bf) added both `valid/schemas/satisfy_singular.gql` and
`invalid/schemas/satisfy_ambiguous.gql`, and the three `label_satisfy_*.cypher`
queries that drive them. The disagreement IS exercised today; it is just
exercised in a way that reads as settled.

**Undisputed, ready to implement once the fork is settled:** whole-entity plural
rejection (`invalid/label_satisfy_ambiguous.cypher`, `MATCH (p:Person) RETURN p`,
is already the right shape and stays invalid under both answers); property
intersection mirroring `unionProperty` (resolve.go:737-756) with
`[]schema.NodeType` for `[]schema.EdgeKey`; and the nodeTypes ripple, which the
count of 20 sites / 13 presence-only / 7 value-reading was checked against and
holds.
close_reason: Closed

title: resolver: multi-label edge types are declarable but unreachable from any query spelling
description:
Discovered while designing gqlc-h9n.7; not covered by that bead as written, and
a stricter statement than it makes.

A declared edge type may carry a multi-label label set — `EdgeKey.Label` is a
full `LabelSetKey` and `internal/schema/gql/resolve.go:65` builds it via
`e.labels.Key()`. So `-[:KNOWS&FOLLOWS]->` is a legal declaration.

**There is no query spelling anywhere that reaches it.** Probed against a schema
declaring `EdgeKey{Source:"A" Label:"FOLLOWS&KNOWS" Target:"B"}`:

    match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS]->(b:B) return r.since
        -> RESOLVE ERROR: unknown edge: A-[KNOWS]->B
    match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS:FOLLOWS]->(b:B) return r.since
        -> PARSE ERROR: no viable alternative at input 'match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS:'
    match (a:A)-[r:KNOWS|FOLLOWS]->(b:B) return r.since
        -> RESOLVE ERROR: unknown edge: A-[KNOWS]->B, A-[FOLLOWS]->B

Nodes at least have the `:A:B` conjunction spelling. Edges have nothing: Cypher
edge patterns take `|` as *alternation*, not `:` as conjunction, and
`edgeCandidates` (`internal/resolver/resolve.go:471-487`) hardcodes the
singleton assumption by building `graph.LabelSet{L}.Key()` per label.

So a schema author who writes a multi-label edge type has declared something
**dead** — it parses, it resolves into the schema model, and no query can ever
name it. That is the same silent-wrong-answer shape the gqlc-h9n epic exists to
eliminate, one layer down.

## Fix, and the open question

The resolver half is the same shape as the node fix: replace the exact `Label`
compare with `declared.Label ⊇ queried labels`.

The genuinely open part is the **query surface**, and it should be decided
before implementing: there is no conjunction syntax for edge labels in the
Cypher dialect the parser accepts, so subset matching on `-[r:KNOWS]->` would
mean a bare single label silently selects a multi-label declared type. Decide
whether that is wanted, or whether the honest fix is instead to **reject a
multi-label edge type at schema load** with a named sentinel until a query
spelling exists. The second is cheaper, is consistent with the epic's posture of
converting silent gaps into named ones, and is widenable later.

Note the interaction with gqlc-h9n.7 step 2: if node bindings become plural, the
endpoint components of an edge key become sets too, and that machinery is shared.
Sequence this after that bead or accept duplicated work.
notes: 2026-07-28, autonomous h9n loop: skipped, not started. Two independent reasons. (1) It DEPENDS ON gqlc-h9n.22, which is reserved for an owner decision on precedence and is outside this loop's delegated scope. (2) Its own open question — subset matching on -[r:KNOWS]-> versus rejecting a multi-label edge type at schema load with a named sentinel — is an ADR-shaped call, and this loop's ADR authority covers only h9n.6, h9n.9, h9n.12 and h9n.25. Loop proceeded to the P3s.
close_reason: Closed

title: schema/gql: assert the model collision a semanticCase describes, not just its spelling
description:
A `semanticCase` records a corpus file that parses, resolves, and is still wrong
because the model has no field for what the parse discarded — `CHAR(4)` resolving
to the same `PropertyType` as bare `CHAR`. Eleven are declared, citing
`gqlc-h9n.16`, `gqlc-h9n.3`, `gqlc-h9n.4` or `gqlc-8pe`.

As of PR #392 each case pins its **spelling**: `TestCorpusManifest` requires the
named file to still contain `"CHAR(4)"`, so the construct cannot be edited out
from under a row that still claims it. That closed the hole where gutting
`scalar_char_fixed_length.gql` left the whole package green at 133/133, 133/133,
46/46. The pin is real, not a declaration row — verified live during the PR #439
review by mutating `scalar_bytes.gql` from `BYTES(1, 10)` to `BYTES(1,10)`, which
goes red at `corpus_test.go:361`.

What is still unpinned is the **collision itself** — that the two spellings really
do resolve to the same model. Nothing in the tree asserts it. If `PropertyType`
silently gained a width field tomorrow, all eleven rows would keep passing while
describing a blind spot that had closed, and the PR body would keep citing them as
evidence of a limit that no longer exists.

## Fix

Parse the semantic-case file and each spelling it must currently resolve
identically to, and `require.Equal` the resolved models. The pairing has to be
declared rather than inferred (the sibling is not always the bare form, and not
always an existing file), and must accommodate equivalence classes of ≥3 members
(see the design section below), so it is a `siblings []string` field alongside
`spelling`.

| semantic case | siblings it must currently equal | bead |
|---|---|---|
| `scalar_char_fixed_length.gql` (`CHAR(4)`) | `["CHAR"]` (bare, in `scalar_character_string.gql`'s `c_bare :: CHAR`) | h9n.16 |
| `scalar_decimal_precision_scale.gql` (`DECIMAL(10,2)`) | `["DEC"]` (in `scalar_dec_alias.gql`) | h9n.16 |
| `scalar_string_max_length.gql` (`STRING(5)`) | `["STRING"]` (bare carrier — file may need to be added) | h9n.16 |
| `scalar_string_min_max_length.gql` (`STRING(2, 5)`) | `["STRING"]` (ditto) | h9n.16 |
| `scalar_varchar_max_length.gql` (`VARCHAR(10)`) | `["VARCHAR"]` (bare carrier — file may need to be added) | h9n.16 |
| `scalar_binary_fixed_length.gql` (`BINARY(4)`) | `["BINARY"]` (bare carrier — file may need to be added) | h9n.4 |
| `scalar_varbinary_max_length.gql` (`VARBINARY(10)`) | `["VARBINARY"]` (bare carrier — file may need to be added) | h9n.4 |
| `scalar_bytes_max_length.gql` (`BYTES(10)`) | `["BYTES"]` (bare carrier — file may need to be added) | h9n.4 |
| `scalar_bytes_min_max_length.gql` (`BYTES(1, 10)`) | `["BYTES"]` (ditto) | h9n.4 |
| `scalar_duration_year_month.gql` (`DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH)`) | `["DURATION(DAY TO SECOND)"]` — widens when `DURATION(DAY TO HOUR)` is added, without a schema change | 8pe |
| `kind_undirected_arc_directed.gql` | **not in the equality loop** — this row is a different shape entirely (accepted-where-should-be-rejected, not X-resolves-equal-to-Y); `siblings: nil`, assertion filed separately | h9n.3 |

## Sibling design: `siblings []string`, not a scalar

Every pre-`3625f89` row pairs `X(n)` against a bare `X` carrier — the sibling
concept reads naturally as "the un-annotated spelling". The four byte-string rows
fit that shape (though several need a carrier that does not yet exist). The
DURATION pair does not fit it at all: the collision is `DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH)`
against `DURATION(DAY TO SECOND)`, two *qualified* spellings colliding with each
other. Bare `DURATION` is a syntax error — PR #439's
`TestPropertyBareDurationRejectedAtParse` pins that — so the sibling cannot be the
bare form.

**A scalar `sibling string` handles the today-known DURATION pair but does not
compose.** The two DURATION spellings today are two members of a partition of
DURATION spellings into equivalence classes over "same populated
`dbtype.Duration` subset". `DURATION(DAY TO HOUR)` will be a third member of the
DAY/SECOND class; adding it to the corpus later must not require a *second*
h9n.21 amendment. So the field is `siblings []string` from day one:

```go
row := semanticSibling{
    spelling: "DURATION(YEAR TO MONTH)",
    siblings: []string{"DURATION(DAY TO SECOND)"}, // widens to add DAY-HOUR etc without schema change
}
// assertion: for _, s := range row.siblings { require.Equal(t, model(row.spelling), model(s)) }
```

The nine existing `h9n.16` / `h9n.4` rows degenerate to a one-element slice
(`siblings: []string{"CHAR"}` etc.) — reads no worse than today's scalar field
would have.

**Alternative not preferred:** a `class string` label with rows sharing a class
value asserted mutually equal. Reads better with ≥3 members but introduces a new
concept; the `[]string` approach handles the same widening without one.

**Explicitly out of the equality loop: `kind_undirected_arc_directed`.** That row
is a third shape entirely — not "X resolves equal to Y" but "X is accepted where
it should be rejected". Its `siblings` slice is `nil`, and the required assertion
for it is filed separately (a rejection check on the parser side, not an equality
on resolved models). Folding it into the equality loop would either mask the real
defect or turn the loop into a two-mode conditional that erodes the pin's clarity.

## Why the assertion is worth more than it looks

It inverts the signal. Today a semantic case is a promise that something is
broken, checked by nobody. With the equality asserted, **the test fails when the
bead lands** — the model gains its field, the two spellings stop resolving
identically, `require.Equal` goes red, and the case gets deleted. That is the same
red-green shape `wantCorpusResolving` already gives for support progress, applied
to the one class of defect coverage can never see.

Follow-up from PR #392 review (finding Q1-E, fix 2). Fix 1 — the spelling pin —
landed in that PR.

## Amendment (PR #392 review, rev-claims final pass)

The reviewer probed the spelling pin for three routes past it. Route 1 is now
closed in #392; routes 2 and 3 belong here, because both close properly only by
asserting the collision.

1. **Comment satisfies the pin.** `require.Contains` read the whole file, so a
   header quoting `CHAR(4)` stood in for GQL that no longer contained it. **Fixed
   in #392** (`546d6da`): the pin now matches against a lexer-stripped copy, so
   none of GQL's three comment forms can carry a spelling on the code's behalf.
   Mutation-tested 6 cases x 4 variants, 24/24 caught; with the strip reverted,
   18 of the 24 escape.
2. **Degenerate spelling.** `spelling: "A"` on the `CHAR(4)` case passes. Nothing
   requires a spelling to discriminate anything — only that it appears. Asserting
   the collision makes the spelling's job checkable: the sibling pair either
   resolves identically or it does not, regardless of what string was declared.
3. **Delete the case wholesale.** Removing the `semanticCase` row along with the
   entry's `bead`/`reason` is green. So the *count* of declared blind spots is
   self-declared: deleting a semantic case is indistinguishable from never having
   had one. Same class as the corpus-dilution gap — adding a file that covers
   nothing is also unpoliced. **Symmetric hole, same shape:** adding a semantic
   case whose collision no equality-assertion covers is equally unpoliced — which
   is exactly what the five rows added by PR #439 would have been without this
   amendment.

Correctly caught already, and worth not regressing: a `semanticCase` naming an
`unsupported` file. The `wrongModel`/`semanticFiles` `ElementsMatch` rejects it,
because a semantic case must by definition resolve.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #461. Added semanticCase.siblings []string + TestSemanticCaseCollisions: each case's file is parsed with each sibling spelling substituted in, and the resolved schema.Schema values must be equal. Substituting into the case's own comment-blanked source means no second corpus file and no bare-carrier files to invent. Added wantSemanticCases to close the delete-the-row route. Three routes mutation-swept and caught. Two findings: bare DECIMAL cannot be a sibling (GQL.g4:1832 puts notNull? inside the parenthesised group, so DECIMAL NOT NULL is not GQL — DECIMAL(8) isolates the same discard); and the bead's kind_undirected_arc_directed row is stale, it became an unsupported entry under gqlc-h9n.3, so the sibling-less shape has no instance and siblings is required non-empty.

title: spec: config-multi-target §8.2 calls three fields distinguishing; only one is
description:
§8.2's prefill paragraph blanks `queries`, `gen.go.out` and `gen.go.package` in
an appended target and calls them "the three that must distinguish it". Only
`gen.go.out` must. The same document's §11 says so in as many words:

  Cross-entry checks beyond output overlap. Shared query directories,
  repeated package names, and repeated schema paths are all legal.

Verified: two entries sharing `queries` and `package` with distinct `out` load
cleanly (2 targets, no error). So the document contradicts itself, and the
false half is the one the implementation comment was copied from — the wording
now also sits in internal/cli/init.go's addPrefill doc comment and in
cli-stage-2.md §3.5, both inherited verbatim from §8.2 on branch 4.

The BEHAVIOUR is right and stays: blank is still the honest prefill for all
three, because a second target usually wants its own query directory and
package even though nothing forces it. Only the justification is wrong — 'must
distinguish' should be 'that a second target normally gives its own', with the
`out` requirement stated separately as the one the loader enforces.

Fix in three places: config-multi-target.md §8.2, cli-stage-2.md §3.5,
init.go's addPrefill comment. Prose only, no code change.

Same class as gqlc-5ta: a merged spec sentence that the branch's own evidence
falsifies.
close_reason: prose fixed in 3 places; PR #545 merged

title: cli: pin the blank-out prompt case in the init wizard
description:

whitespace-only) `out` at the prompt.

Found by the branch-4 review (gqlc-0gb.4), reproduced on a scratch

- dropping the post-form trim of `Go.Out` (§4.2's trim)
- swapping the two checks inside `validateOut`
